client: I've been feeling really on edge lately with my final exams coming up next month. My statistics class has been especially difficult, and I keep worrying that no matter how much I study, I'll fail the exam. The pressure just keeps building and I can't seem to relax or focus properly.
therapist: It sounds like exam pressures, especially in statistics, are really weighing on you. The way you described this makes me hear both the worry about studying effectively and the physical tension that comes with it. Have you noticed any particular times when the stress feels more manageable or less intense?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I do feel a little better when I'm studying with classmates, but then I start comparing myself to them and thinking I'm falling behind. The stress comes right back, especially when I see how quickly some people seem to understand the material. It's like my brain freezes up when I try to study alone, but studying with others brings its own kind of anxiety.
therapist: It sounds like studying with others gives you some relief, but then those comparison thoughts creep in and bring the anxiety back. I notice you describe this back-and-fort experience with a mix of hope and frustration—what do you make of that pattern?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client:
Yeah, that's exactly it. When I'm actually studying with people, I feel okay in the moment—like maybe I can keep up. But then someone mentions their grades or study habits, and I immediately start thinking I'm way behind. The hope comes from wanting that connection, but the frustration is that it never lasts. 

I don't know if this pattern can really change. Even if I try to ignore those thoughts, they feel so automatic. Like my brain just defaults to comparing myself no matter what.
therapist: You're describing this push-and-pull so clearly—the temporary relief of connection followed by those automatic comparison thoughts that steal your confidence. I hear how exhausting this cycle feels when you say "it never lasts," and I'm curious, what do those moments feel like right before the comparison thoughts kick in?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client:
It's like this brief moment of calm where I actually feel okay—like I belong in the conversation or that I'm interesting enough. But then it's like my brain just can't let me have that peace. I start noticing little things—how someone laughs at their joke more than mine, or how they seem more put together—and the anxiety creeps back in. 

I don't know why I can't just stay in that good moment. It makes me not even want to try connecting with people because I know the crash is coming.
therapist: I hear both the fleeting sweetness of those calm moments and the painful anticipation of the crash that follows—it makes so much sense that you'd want to protect yourself from that rollercoaster. When you're in that space where you briefly feel you belong, what's different about how you're seeing yourself in those moments compared to when the comparisons start?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client:
In those rare moments when I feel like I belong, I guess I stop seeing myself as this outsider looking in. I don't analyze every little thing I say or wonder if I'm being judged. But then the fear creeps back in - like I'm just fooling myself and it's only a matter of time before people realize I don't really fit in. 

It's hard to hold onto that good feeling because part of me believes it's not real, that I'm just temporarily tricking people into thinking I'm normal. The more I try to enjoy it, the louder that doubting voice gets.
therapist: You've described so clearly how that sense of belonging gets overshadowed by the fear of being "found out"—it's like you can't trust those peaceful moments because part of you believes they're just an illusion. I wonder what it would be like to notice that doubting voice without letting it rewrite the whole experience?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I want to trust those moments, but it's like my brain automatically finds reasons they aren't real. Like if coworkers invite me to lunch, I'll spend the whole time thinking they're just being polite or feel sorry for me. It makes me feel stupid for even wanting to believe it's genuine.
therapist: It sounds like those invitations from coworkers bring up such a painful tug-of-war—part of you wants to accept the connection, while another part insists it must be pity. I can hear how exhausting it feels to constantly question people's motives. When those doubts creep in during lunch, what typically happens to your ability to be present in the conversation?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client:
I usually just shut down when the doubts take over during lunch. My mind races trying to analyze if they really want me there, and then I can't focus on what anyone's saying. It makes me feel even more isolated because I'm physically present but mentally a million miles away. 

Sometimes I wonder if I'm just making it worse by overthinking everything. But how do I stop when it feels so obvious they're just being polite?
therapist: You're describing such a painful cycle—physically being there while mentally checking out, which then reinforces that sense of isolation. I notice you mentioned it feels "obvious" they're just being polite—what would it be like to consider that your interpretation might be coloring the situation, rather than being an absolute truth?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I get what you're saying, but it's hard to believe people actually want me around when they never reach out first. My brain keeps going back to all the times I've been left out or forgotten - it feels like proof that I'm just not that important to them. Even when I try to challenge those thoughts, the evidence feels overwhelming.
therapist: I hear how painful it is to carry these experiences of being left out—they feel like undeniable proof that you don't matter to others. When those memories come up so vividly, what's it like to sit with both the hurt they bring and the possibility that they might not tell the whole story about your worth?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: It’s hard to sit with those memories because they feel so real and overwhelming. When I think about being left out, it’s like my brain just loops the same story—that I’m not important enough for anyone to care about. I guess I can see that there might be other explanations, but it’s hard to believe them when the hurt feels so sharp and immediate.
therapist: You're describing how those painful memories create such a strong, immediate reaction—one that overshadows other possible explanations even when you can recognize they exist. I notice you said this with a mix of sadness and resignation—would you be willing to explore what makes that particular story about not being important feel so convincing to you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: It just feels like the obvious truth, you know? Like when people forget to invite me or cancel plans last minute—it keeps happening, so it's hard not to take it personally. I try to tell myself it's not about me, but the feeling of being unimportant always wins.
therapist: I can hear how deeply these repeated experiences have convinced you of this painful story about yourself—there's a real heaviness in your voice when you describe how the feeling of being unimportant "always wins." What does it feel like in your body when that belief takes over after someone cancels plans?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
